author: ohtadmin
title: Help celebrate Ukrainian culture Saturday
text:
A festival to celebrate the culture and citizens of Ukraine will commemorate its fifth anniversary in 2026 by continuing to raise money for the country during the war with Russia.
The Jamestown Ukraine Relief Project will sponsor its fifth annual Sunflower Family Festival from 11 a.m. to 2 p.m. Saturday, Aug. 22, at Lawn School. Admission to the event, which is named for Ukraine’s national flower, is free.
The event honors the traditions of Ukraine in America as the country in Europe celebrates its independence day, which is Aug. 24. Consistent with its sunflower motif and family focus, the festival is “keyed to themes of hope and vibrant celebration, sharing the positive vision of a Ukraine free and at peace, and providing views of an extraordinarily beautiful country and its people.”
The festival will offer crafts, face painting, hair braiding and pysanky (Ukrainian Easter eggs) with music by Snailhand, the South County Rounders, the Kumis family and flautist Sasha Pinchuk. Food will include Polish pierogis, golabki (stuffed cabbage) and kielbasa.
Proceeds from the silent auction and raffles will support Voices of Children, which is the largest Ukrainian foundation providing comprehensive psychological support to children living through war. The charity has centers in 10 Ukrainian cities, primarily in frontline areas, which offer safe, welcoming and enriching environments for children.
One of the children helped by the organization is Matvii Berezhnyi, 15, who is from Kharkiv Oblast. He has survived missile attack after missile attack from the Russians.
“The war has made many of us grow up faster,” he said. “Not just me.”
During one of the missile attacks, Matvii’s mother was injured while she was delivering food to Ukrainian soldiers at a checkpoint. In another, a cluster bomb hit their home.
“It was really scary, but we made it through,” he said. “A streetlight pole saved me when the cluster bomb struck it. I was only about 10 feet away. If it weren’t for that pole, I might not be here now.”
In 2024, Matvii attended a camp in Zakarpattia, organized by the Voices of Children in partnership with the Olena Zelenska Foundation. There, he was able to rest, make friends and begin to heal emotionally after everything he had endured.
“I’m always impressed by how these kids, even after everything, somehow don’t lose their childlike spirit,” said Illia Valkov, a camp mentor. “They might talk about something heartbreaking in a psychology session, and 10 minutes later they’re running around and laughing. They switch so fast.”
Matvii loves sports and dreams of learning about investing. One day, he hopes to buy a car and travel the world with his family.
Another Ukrainian child, Kira, woke up to loud explosions in February 2022. She was 8.
“At first, I didn’t understand what was going on, but my mother was alarmed and the explosions were repeated,” she said. “My brother, mother, grandmother and our dog gathered in my grandmother’s room. I climbed under the table with the dog, we put the lamp and sat there. I remember how a rocket flew over the house. We could hear a whistle, and we were very scared, because it could just get into the house.”
Kira often visits the Voices of Children center in Lviv, where she plays board games and participates in a psychological group.
“I never want to miss these meetings,” she said. “There is a very cool space here with kind people who can always help if something happens or just need to talk. It helps a lot. I started talking more, it became easier for me to meet new people.”
Since March 2022, the Jamestown Ukraine Relief Project has provided more than $200,000 in support of humanitarian relief efforts, advocacy and rebuilding efforts for Ukraine and its people. Initial aid money went to direct relief organizations, such as Doctors Without Borders, World Central Kitchen and Razom for Ukraine.
The 501(c)3 corporation, headquartered at Central Baptist Church, is a nondenominational, nonpolitical group. It is led by John Andrews, Mary Jan Krause- Greene, Eleanor Howard, Wayne Cresser, Betsy Parsons and Karen Buetens.
The town council is encouraging the community to attend the festival, and Aug. 23 was designated as Sunflower Family Festival Day through a proclamation passed unanimously Monday by the councilors.
The event, according to the proclamation, allows Jamestown resident “to demonstrate their support and admiration for the people of Ukraine in their ongoing and painful struggle for freedom, and “warmly welcomes and salutes Rhode Island’s new Ukrainian immigrants and the decades-long contributions of our Ukrainian-American neighbors to the vitality, cultural heritage and civic life.”
